transcript.content: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, I suppose the main thing is that I’ve noticed I just don’t seem to stay seated when other people do. It sounds small when I say it out loud, but it’s become a bit embarrassing. In meetings at school, or even at dinner, I’ll suddenly get up—like I’ll decide I need to refill my coffee, or check a handout, or walk to the back of the room for some reason. And often, when I think about it afterward, there really wasn’t anything urgent at all. Everyone else is just sitting and carrying on, and I’m the one popping up and moving around. That’s what made me think I should come in and talk to someone about it.
When you were a child, were you often described as fidgety or unable to stay seated?

Yes, very much so. I mean, looking back, it was one of those things that was sort of part of the family story, if that makes sense. My report cards were always, “She’s bright,” or “She understands the work,” but then there would be that “but” afterward—“but she doesn’t stay in her seat,” or “but she has trouble waiting her turn.” I remember seeing those comments more than once.

And my mother used to laugh about it, though I think she was also a bit worn out by it. She’d say I must have worn a path in the floor between my desk and the pencil sharpener before I was even ten, because I was constantly getting up for some reason. Sharpening a pencil, asking something, moving around—anything rather than just sitting there like the other children seemed able to do. At the time I don’t think I saw it as unusual, but yes, apparently other people definitely noticed.
Do you often have trouble sustaining your attention on tasks or conversations?

I’m not sure I’d say that’s the main thing, no. I mean, I do sometimes lose the thread if something is very dry or if someone is going on for a long time, but I’ve always thought that was fairly normal, especially after a full day of teaching.

With tasks, if I know what I’m doing and there’s a clear purpose to it, I can usually keep with it. And in conversations, I don’t generally feel as though I’m drifting away or unable to follow, unless I’m already tired or the conversation is terribly slow. It’s more that I feel uncomfortable sitting still through the whole thing, if that makes sense. But in terms of attention itself—sustaining it—I haven’t really noticed that as a major problem.
When you’re sitting and then get up, does it usually feel like an inner physical restlessness that builds up until you move?

Yes, I think that’s a fair way to put it. It’s not usually that I have some very sensible reason to stand up, though at the time I dress it up as one. I’ll be in a staff meeting, for example, and suddenly I’ll think, “Oh, I should just refill my coffee,” or “I need to look at that handout at the back,” or I’ll get up to check something that really could have waited.

It’s more like sitting there starts to feel almost… uncomfortable, not painful, but like my body is insisting I do something. And then once I’m up, there’s a bit of relief, even if I realize afterward that there wasn’t actually anything urgent. The embarrassing part is that everyone else is still seated, perfectly normal, carrying on with the meeting or dinner, and I’m the one who has popped up again for no especially good reason.
When you feel the need to get up, is it because you’re trying to quiet a particular worry or intrusive thought?

No, I don’t think so. At least, that’s not how it feels to me.

It isn’t like I’m sitting there thinking, “If I don’t get up, something bad will happen,” or trying to push away a particular thought. It’s more physical than mental, if that makes sense. I might have thoughts attached to it afterward—like inventing a reason to get up, or telling myself I need to fetch something—but I wouldn’t say there’s a worry underneath it that I’m trying to quiet.

I suppose there are times when I’m stressed and I’m probably more restless, but the urge to move doesn’t seem to come from one specific fear or intrusive idea. It’s just this sort of internal pressure to be up and doing something.
Have you ever had a period when your mood was unusually high, euphoric, or unusually irritable for you?

I don’t think so, no. I mean, I’ve certainly had good moods and bad moods like anyone else, and I can be a bit sharp if I’m tired or if the day has been especially trying, but I wouldn’t say there’s been a period where I felt unusually euphoric or not myself in that way.

And with irritability… I suppose teaching can make anyone irritable at times, especially after years of it, but it feels understandable to the situation rather than some separate change in my mood. I haven’t noticed anything where people around me would say, “You’re acting completely different,” or where I felt suddenly high or unusually driven by my mood. So, no—not that I’m aware of.
Do you ever have sudden movements or sounds that happen over and over, like blinking, shrugging, throat-clearing, or other tics?

I don’t think so, no. Not in the way you’re describing, at least.

I mean, I might clear my throat if I’ve been talking all day, which I do quite a lot as a teacher, or blink more if my eyes are tired, but I wouldn’t say I have a repeated movement or sound that just happens on its own over and over. I’ve never had anyone point out that I’m shrugging or twitching or making noises, and it’s not something I’ve noticed in myself.

So, no—nothing I’d recognize as tics, unless there’s something more subtle you mean.
Do you often find yourself worrying excessively about many different areas of your life?

I’m not sure I’d say excessively, no. I mean, I do worry about ordinary things—work, whether I’ve handled something properly with a student, family bits and pieces, practical things that need doing—but I don’t feel as though I’m constantly worrying across lots of areas of my life in a way that takes over.

Sometimes I’ll go over something in my head more than I need to, especially if it’s been a busy day, but it doesn’t feel like this broad, uncontrollable worrying about everything. It’s more just… normal concerns, I think. Unless I’m underestimating it, but I wouldn’t describe myself as a chronic worrier.

final_diagnosis.reason: The interview supports attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder, predominantly hyperactive presentation/in type, with a persistent pattern of hyperactivity-restlessness since childhood and continuing into adulthood. The patient clearly endorses difficulty remaining seated, frequent getting up in situations where remaining seated is expected, and subjective inner physical restlessness relieved by movement. Childhood onset is supported by repeated school report comments and parental observations before age 10. Inattention is not prominent, but ICD-10 F90.0 encompasses hyperkinetic disorder/ADHD and is the only supported candidate provided. Alternative explanations explored were not supported: no intrusive-thought-driven compulsion, no manic/hypomanic mood change, no tic disorder, and no excessive generalized worry.
